name: usbtree
desc: Live USB device tree in your terminal
why: A live view of the USB topology reveals hidden hub and device structure most people never see, a gentle door into the bus.

brief.what_it_is: usbtree is a cross-platform terminal UI (TUI) that shows your USB device tree live: hubs, device classes, link speeds, hot-plug events, and bandwidth. It reads the USB bus directly through the nusb Rust library, with no libusb and no root needed for the basic tree. Output is an interactive tree on screen, plus a --dump flag for scripts. A --demo flag shows the interface without hardware. It is distributed as one static binary per OS, with prebuilt releases for Linux, macOS and Windows.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage positions it as 'Everything lsusb -t shows, plus names that make sense, hot-plug awareness, and live traffic.' It aims to make the USB topology visible and readable without needing lsusb or manual lookups.
brief.how_it_works: Names are resolved through a chain: your overrides.ids file, then device descriptor strings, then a downloadable usb.ids (via --updatelist), then an embedded snapshot, then vendor and class heuristics. The tree rescans every second, and hot-plugged devices flash green while unplugged ones linger as red crossed-out ghosts for 30 seconds, logged in an events panel. Live bandwidth is unprivileged URBs/s on Linux, and real bytes/s when run as root with the usbmon module loaded. Misc/IAD composite devices are classified by their interface classes.

commands_seen.context: Shell installer for Linux and macOS; installs to /usr/local/bin or ~/.local/bin, verifies checksums.
Runs the TUI with simulated devices so you can try it without USB hardware.
Homebrew install on Linux or Apple Silicon macOS, using the prebuilt binary.
PowerShell installer for Windows; installs to %LOCALAPPDATA%\usbtree\bin and adds it to PATH.
Manual install from a release archive, then run the binary directly.
On macOS, removes the quarantine flag from a manually downloaded binary, since binaries are not notarized.
Builds and installs from source with Cargo; needs a stable toolchain with edition 2024.
Builds a release binary from a cloned repository.

brief.install_notes: Install options: Homebrew (Linux and Apple Silicon macOS only), shell script (Linux and macOS, pin with USBTREE_VERSION, override directory with USBTREE_INSTALL_DIR), PowerShell (Windows, pin with $env:USBTREE_VERSION), manual release archive, or Cargo from source. Prebuilt archives exist for linux-amd64, linux-arm64, darwin-arm64 and windows-amd64, and checksums are listed in checksums.txt. The installers need a published GitHub release; if none exists yet, install from source. No accounts or runtimes are required. Real per-device bytes/s on Linux needs root plus the usbmon kernel module. Safe eject uses udisks2 on Linux.
brief.standout: It is a live, color-coded USB tree in the terminal with friendly vendor and device names, hot-plug ghosts, and sparklines, all in one static binary with no libusb. The composite-device handling is notable: a MOTU audio interface shows as Audio instead of Misc, and it can safely eject USB drives without root through udisks2. It also has a PCI view toggled with p.
brief.status: unknown. The homepage gives no release date, version number or last-commit date, and I did not fetch the GitHub repository or releases page to check. It does describe a current feature set and install paths that refer to a published release.
brief.caveats: Live per-device traffic and real bandwidth are Linux-only; macOS and Windows expose no unprivileged per-device counter, and sudo does not help there. Safe eject is Linux-only for now. Prebuilt binaries are not code-signed or notarized: macOS needs xattr to clear quarantine, and Windows SmartScreen may warn on first run. Prebuilt binaries are not offered for Intel macOS (only darwin-arm64 is listed). Building from source needs a stable Rust toolchain supporting edition 2024. The homepage is the only page I read; the README and docs were not fetched.
